newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korea's reliance on nuclear power to grow.
newsitem.headline: South Korea's reliance on nuclear power to grow.

text.p: South Korea's lack of natural resources and pollution concerns are forcing the country to boost its reliance on nuclear energy, government officials and analysts said on Monday.
"South Korea's policy is to continue raising nuclear power generation capacity into the year 2010," said a senior official in charge of nuclear power generation at the energy ministry.
"Nuclear power is cheaper and cleaner than other power resources such as gas and oil and more economical than electric power which we have to rely on mother nature for," he said.

The government plans to expand South Korea's total installed nuclear power capacity to 13,716 megawatts by 2000 and 26,329 megawatts by 2010, which would constitute 38 percent and 46 percent respectively of total power production.

The recent completion of the nation's 12th nuclear power station, the 700-megawatt Wolsung-2, will raise total capacity to more than 10,000 megawatts at the end of June when it starts commercial operation. This is equivalent to 36 percent of total national power generation.
The state-run Korea Electric Power Corp (KEPCO) has a monopoly in South Korea's nuclear power generation. The government has a 75 percent stake in KEPCO.

"Six nuclear power plants are currently under construction which we expect to complete between 1998-2002," the ministry official said. Two have a 700-megawatt capacity and the others have a capacity of 1,000 megawatts each.
"We plan to build 10 more nuclear power plants by 2010. But everything remains flexible."
Analysts said South Korea's growing dependence on nuclear power was inevitable considering the country's lack of natural resources. The nation imports 95 percent of its energy demand.
"Nuclear power generation is the most efficient way to generate power," said Bill Hunsaker, energy analyst at ING-Barings Securities.
"Uranium imports are cheaper than that of other fuel and have little impact on the trade deficit."
Nuclear energy, coal, liquefied natural gas, fuel oil, gas oil and hydroelectric power are used to generate electricity.
Despite costly construction fees and possible environmental risks, nuclear power stations cost less to run and the energy output level is high.
Analysts and government officials said South Korea's policy was unlikely to be affected by domestic protests or crumbling nuclear policies in industrialised countries such as Japan and France.

"We expect some protests from people in the neighbourhoods of proposed sites for nuclear power stations," said the ministry official. "But the projects will continue regardless of the protests," he said.
Lobbying efforts to oppose nuclear facilities have not been fruitful in South Korea, analysts said.
"The lobby concept is not big in Korea," said Hunsaker at ING-Barings. "There have been some protests but they haven't been very successful."
Japan's nuclear energy reputation has come under criticism because of a litany of accidents and cover-ups.
France scrapped a plan for a fault-prone nuclear fast-breeder last week -- another blow to its government's efforts to develop nuclear power.
Although figures for nuclear accidents in South Korea are not available, some troubles have come to light, sparking strong protests.
Last August, the 950-megawatt plant in Yongwang in southwestern South Korea was closed for almost a month after a radiation leakage.
"Nuclear power projects are very dangerous and further plans need to be scrapped," said Park Sang-cheol, director of the Korean Federation for Enviromental Movement.
